claims.text: The applicable alloy is equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi alloy is a simple, single-phase solid solution.
The starting alloy has good ductility and machinability but low hardness and strength.
High chemical disorder in the starting solid solution facilitates easy dislocation nucleation.
The low hardness and strength are governed by rapid dynamic recovery, enhanced cross-slip, or dislocation annihilation.
Heat-treatment parameters can be tailored to induce or control nanoscale precipitates.
A tailored heat treatment can induce short-range order in CoCrFeNiTi without substantially changing its overall composition.
Short-range-order regions create barriers to dislocation activity.
Nanoscale precipitates act as barriers or pinning points for dislocation motion.
Facile dislocation nucleation and recovery prevent substantial dislocation pile-up and strain hardening in the untreated alloy.
Increasing short-range order raises the barrier to dislocation nucleation or activity and increases strength.
Induced precipitates or short-range order slow recovery and promote dislocation accumulation.
The heat-treated alloy will have greater hardness and yield strength than the untreated alloy.
The heat-treated alloy will exhibit altered strain-hardening behavior, potentially including a higher work-hardening rate.
The proposed comparison uses untreated and heat-treated samples tested under identical tensile, hardness, temperature, and strain-rate conditions.
The proposed mechanism is restricted to conditions under which dislocation-mediated plasticity dominates.
The precipitate size, distribution, and coherency, and the magnitude of strengthening, depend sensitively on treatment parameters.
Failure to observe a statistically significant increase in hardness and yield strength or any change in strain hardening would falsify the proposed baseline dislocation-dynamics mechanism.

contradictions.description: The boundary requires CoCrFeNiTi to remain in a single-phase solid-solution state, whereas the proposed precipitation intervention would ordinarily produce a matrix-plus-precipitate multiphase state. Short-range ordering could remain compatible with a single phase, but precipitation is not.
